additions.title: Numerator and denominator
additions.objective: Identify the roles of fraction components

content.body: In three quarters, three counts selected parts and four names the number of equal parts in the whole. The denominator also tells you the size of each part relative to that whole.

quickCheck.prompt: In three quarters, what does three count?
options: All the parts in the whole
quickCheck.explanation: Selected equal parts. In three quarters, three counts selected parts and four names the number of equal parts in the whole. The denominator also tells you the size of each part relative to that whole.

additions.title: Fraction vocabulary
additions.objective: Distinguish a unit fraction from other fractions

content.body: A unit fraction has numerator one, such as one fifth. It names one of the equal parts made by dividing a whole; three fifths contains three of those unit fractions.

quickCheck.prompt: Which is a unit fraction?
quickCheck.explanation: One fifth. A unit fraction has numerator one, such as one fifth. It names one of the equal parts made by dividing a whole; three fifths contains three of those unit fractions.

additions.title: The reference whole
additions.objective: Keep the reference whole explicit

content.body: Half of a small orange and half of a large orange are the same fraction of different wholes. They need not have the same mass. State the whole whenever comparing fractional quantities.

quickCheck.prompt: Must half of a small orange have the same mass as half of a large orange?
quickCheck.explanation: No, the reference wholes differ. Half of a small orange and half of a large orange are the same fraction of different wholes. They need not have the same mass. State the whole whenever comparing fractional quantities.

additions.title: Equal-area model
additions.objective: Interpret equal-area fraction models

content.body: The model divides one rectangle into four equal areas and shades three of them. It represents three quarters of that rectangle; equal part sizes make the denominator meaningful.

quickCheck.prompt: Three of four equal areas are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
quickCheck.explanation: Three quarters. The model divides one rectangle into four equal areas and shades three of them. It represents three quarters of that rectangle; equal part sizes make the denominator meaningful.

additions.title: Worked sharing example
additions.objective: Explain a fraction-of-a-quantity method

content.body: To find three quarters of twelve counters, first divide twelve into four equal groups of three. Then select three groups, giving nine counters. Recombining the selected nine and remaining three gives twelve.

quickCheck.prompt: What is three quarters of twelve?
quickCheck.explanation: Nine. To find three quarters of twelve counters, first divide twelve into four equal groups of three. Then select three groups, giving nine counters. Recombining the selected nine and remaining three gives twelve.

additions.title: The compared quantities
additions.objective: Identify the quantities and their order in a ratio

content.body: A ratio must identify which quantities are compared and in which order. In a flour-to-water ratio of three to two, the first quantity is flour and the second is water; reversing the order changes the description.

quickCheck.prompt: In flour to water of three to two, which quantity has three parts?
quickCheck.explanation: Flour. A ratio must identify which quantities are compared and in which order. In a flour-to-water ratio of three to two, the first quantity is flour and the second is water; reversing the order changes the description.

additions.title: Parts and consistent units
additions.objective: Use consistent units in ratio comparisons

content.body: To compare fifty centimetres with one metre, first express both lengths in the same unit. Fifty to one hundred simplifies to one to two. Treating the units as equal without conversion gives a different and incorrect comparison.

quickCheck.prompt: Fifty centimetres to one metre simplifies to what?
quickCheck.explanation: One to two. To compare fifty centimetres with one metre, first express both lengths in the same unit. Fifty to one hundred simplifies to one to two. Treating the units as equal without conversion gives a different and incorrect comparison.

additions.title: A multiplicative comparison
additions.objective: Explain ratio as a multiplicative relationship

content.body: A two-to-three comparison describes a relationship that can be scaled. Four to six and six to nine preserve it because both quantities change by the same factor. The total quantity can vary while the ratio stays fixed.

quickCheck.prompt: Which preserves a two-to-three relationship?
quickCheck.explanation: Four to six. A two-to-three comparison describes a relationship that can be scaled. Four to six and six to nine preserve it because both quantities change by the same factor. The total quantity can vary while the ratio stays fixed.

additions.title: Ratio model
additions.objective: Connect a ratio model to part-to-whole fractions

content.body: The model has two green counters and three blue counters. Green to blue is two to three, while green to the whole group is two to five. These comparisons answer different questions.

quickCheck.prompt: What fraction of the five-counter group is green?
quickCheck.explanation: Two fifths. The model has two green counters and three blue counters. Green to blue is two to three, while green to the whole group is two to five. These comparisons answer different questions.

additions.title: Worked ratio share
additions.objective: Calculate a ratio share using one part

content.body: Share twenty counters in a one-to-three ratio. There are four parts, so each part contains five counters. The shares are five and fifteen; their sum and simplified ratio both check the result.

quickCheck.prompt: Twenty counters are shared in a one-to-three ratio. What is the smaller share?
quickCheck.explanation: Five. Share twenty counters in a one-to-three ratio. There are four parts, so each part contains five counters. The shares are five and fifteen; their sum and simplified ratio both check the result.

additions.title: Percent, part and whole
additions.objective: Identify percentage components

content.body: A percentage comparison has a part, a reference whole and a rate per hundred. If ten of forty learners cycle, ten is the part and forty is the whole. The percentage is twenty-five.

quickCheck.prompt: Ten of forty learners cycle. Which value is the whole?
quickCheck.explanation: Forty. A percentage comparison has a part, a reference whole and a rate per hundred. If ten of forty learners cycle, ten is the part and forty is the whole. The percentage is twenty-five.

additions.title: Percent and percentage points
additions.objective: Use percent and percentage points precisely

content.body: Percent expresses a rate relative to a base. Percentage points express the difference between two percentage rates. Moving from ten percent to fifteen percent adds five percentage points, even though the relative increase is fifty percent.

quickCheck.prompt: From ten percent to fifteen percent is how many percentage points?
quickCheck.explanation: Five. Percent expresses a rate relative to a base. Percentage points express the difference between two percentage rates. Moving from ten percent to fifteen percent adds five percentage points, even though the relative increase is fifty percent.

additions.title: Keep the base visible
additions.objective: Explain why percentage comparisons depend on the base

content.body: Fifty percent of twenty is ten, while fifty percent of two hundred is one hundred. Equal percentages need not mean equal quantities. Identify the original base before comparing the actual changes.

quickCheck.prompt: Do equal percentages of different totals always give equal quantities?
options: Yes, the percentage alone fixes the quantity
quickCheck.explanation: No, the bases also matter. Fifty percent of twenty is ten, while fifty percent of two hundred is one hundred. Equal percentages need not mean equal quantities. Identify the original base before comparing the actual changes.

additions.title: Hundred-square representation
additions.objective: Read a percentage from a hundred-square grid

content.body: A ten-by-ten grid has one hundred equal squares. Shading twenty-five shows twenty-five percent, which is also one quarter of the grid. Each square represents one percent of this whole.

quickCheck.prompt: Twenty-five of one hundred squares are shaded. What percentage is shaded?
quickCheck.explanation: Twenty-five percent. A ten-by-ten grid has one hundred equal squares. Shading twenty-five shows twenty-five percent, which is also one quarter of the grid. Each square represents one percent of this whole.

additions.title: Worked percentage example
additions.objective: Calculate a simple percentage using known parts

content.body: Find fifteen percent of sixty by combining ten percent and five percent. Ten percent is six and five percent is three, so fifteen percent is nine. Check that the answer is less than the whole sixty.

quickCheck.prompt: What is fifteen percent of sixty?
quickCheck.explanation: Nine. Find fifteen percent of sixty by combining ten percent and five percent. Ten percent is six and five percent is three, so fifteen percent is nine. Check that the answer is less than the whole sixty.

additions.title: Why equations are useful
additions.objective: Explain the purpose of an equation model

content.body: An equation represents a condition in which two expressions have equal values. It lets us describe an unknown quantity and find a value that satisfies that condition. A contextual answer must also fit the original situation.

quickCheck.prompt: What must a solution do?
options: Only make one side look simpler
quickCheck.explanation: Make the original equality true. An equation represents a condition in which two expressions have equal values. It lets us describe an unknown quantity and find a value that satisfies that condition. A contextual answer must also fit the original situation.

additions.title: Term, coefficient and variable
additions.objective: Identify equation vocabulary

content.body: In two x plus three equals eleven, x is a variable, two is the coefficient of x, and three is a constant term. Naming these parts helps explain which operation should be undone first.

quickCheck.prompt: In two x plus three, which is the coefficient of x?
quickCheck.explanation: Two. In two x plus three equals eleven, x is a variable, two is the coefficient of x, and three is a constant term. Naming these parts helps explain which operation should be undone first.

additions.title: A reversible procedure
additions.objective: Sequence inverse operations correctly

content.body: For three x plus two equals fourteen, first subtract two from both sides. Then divide both sides by three to obtain x equals four. Finally substitute four into the original equation to check it.

quickCheck.prompt: After subtracting two from both sides, three x equals twelve. What comes next?
options: Subtract three only from the left side
quickCheck.explanation: Divide both sides by three. For three x plus two equals fourteen, first subtract two from both sides. Then divide both sides by three to obtain x equals four. Finally substitute four into the original equation to check it.

additions.title: Recognise equation variations
additions.objective: Recognise equivalent equations in different forms

content.body: An unknown can appear on either side of an equals sign. Eight equals x plus three has the same solution as x plus three equals eight. Read the equality before applying a memorised position rule.

quickCheck.prompt: Does eight equals x plus three have the same solution as x plus three equals eight?
options: No, moving the equals sign changes the solution
Yes, both assert the same equality
quickCheck.explanation: Yes, both assert the same equality. An unknown can appear on either side of an equals sign. Eight equals x plus three has the same solution as x plus three equals eight. Read the equality before applying a memorised position rule.

additions.title: Worked balance example
additions.objective: Justify and check a balance method

content.body: Solve x plus three equals eight by subtracting three from each side. The two sides remain equal and x equals five. Substitution checks that five plus three equals eight.

quickCheck.prompt: Which value solves x plus three equals eight?
quickCheck.explanation: Five. Solve x plus three equals eight by subtracting three from each side. The two sides remain equal and x equals five. Substitution checks that five plus three equals eight.

additions.title: Worked data comparison
additions.objective: Use a graph and its units to compare observations

content.body: The illustrative rainfall graph shows ten, thirty, twenty and forty millimetres over days one to four. Day four has thirty millimetres more rain than day one. The dip on day three means the increase was not continuous.

quickCheck.prompt: Does the rainfall increase on every successive day?
options: No, it falls from day two to day three
Yes, it increases without any fall
quickCheck.explanation: No, it falls from day two to day three. The illustrative rainfall graph shows ten, thirty, twenty and forty millimetres over days one to four. Day four has thirty millimetres more rain than day one. The dip on day three means the increase was not continuous.

additions.title: Purpose and food chains
additions.objective: Explain the biological role of photosynthesis

content.body: Photosynthesis transfers light energy into the chemical stores of organic substances such as glucose. Plants use these substances for growth and respiration, and other organisms can obtain them through feeding relationships. This connects leaves to wider food chains.

quickCheck.prompt: How can photosynthesis support a food chain?
options: It produces organic substances that organisms can use
It makes energy disappear from the ecosystem
quickCheck.explanation: It produces organic substances that organisms can use. Photosynthesis transfers light energy into the chemical stores of organic substances such as glucose. Plants use these substances for growth and respiration, and other organisms can obtain them through feeding relationships. This connects leaves to wider food chains.

additions.title: Limiting factors
additions.objective: Explain why changing one factor may not change the rate

content.body: Light, carbon dioxide and suitable temperature affect photosynthesis. Increasing light helps only when light limits the rate; another factor can prevent a further increase. A plateau is therefore a reason to examine other conditions.

quickCheck.prompt: Must more light always keep increasing the photosynthesis rate?
options: No, another factor can become limiting
quickCheck.explanation: No, another factor can become limiting. Light, carbon dioxide and suitable temperature affect photosynthesis. Increasing light helps only when light limits the rate; another factor can prevent a further increase. A plateau is therefore a reason to examine other conditions.

additions.title: Inputs, energy and outputs
additions.objective: Interpret the photosynthesis process model

content.body: The process model shows carbon dioxide and water entering, light energy being absorbed with the help of chlorophyll, and glucose and oxygen being produced. Light supplies energy rather than atoms of plant material.

quickCheck.prompt: In the model, what role does light play?
options: It supplies energy for the process
It supplies soil particles to the leaf
quickCheck.explanation: It supplies energy for the process. The process model shows carbon dioxide and water entering, light energy being absorbed with the help of chlorophyll, and glucose and oxygen being produced. Light supplies energy rather than atoms of plant material.

additions.title: Compare explanations
additions.objective: Distinguish balanced forces from an absence of forces

content.body: A stationary box can have forces acting on it that balance. Lack of acceleration does not by itself prove that no forces act. Identify the interactions and their directions before choosing an explanation.

quickCheck.prompt: A box remains at rest. Must there be no forces on it?
options: Yes, rest proves the absence of every force
quickCheck.explanation: No, forces can balance. A stationary box can have forces acting on it that balance. Lack of acceleration does not by itself prove that no forces act. Identify the interactions and their directions before choosing an explanation.

additions.title: Evidence from a force diagram
additions.objective: Use a force diagram to justify a resultant

content.body: The diagram represents twelve newtons right and five newtons left. These opposite forces leave a resultant of seven newtons right. The resultant predicts a change in velocity, not an exact current speed.

quickCheck.prompt: What is the resultant shown by twelve newtons right and five newtons left?
quickCheck.explanation: Seven newtons right. The diagram represents twelve newtons right and five newtons left. These opposite forces leave a resultant of seven newtons right. The resultant predicts a change in velocity, not an exact current speed.

additions.title: Purpose of the circuit
additions.objective: Explain a circuit as an energy-transfer system

content.body: A complete circuit connects an electrical source with components that transfer energy, such as lamps. Wires provide conducting paths and switches control whether paths are complete. The source and components have different roles in the system.

quickCheck.prompt: What is a lamp's main role in a circuit?
options: Transfer energy into light and thermal stores
quickCheck.explanation: Transfer energy into light and thermal stores. A complete circuit connects an electrical source with components that transfer energy, such as lamps. Wires provide conducting paths and switches control whether paths are complete. The source and components have different roles in the system.

additions.title: Feedback and control
additions.objective: Distinguish manual switching from automatic feedback

content.body: A simple cell-and-lamp circuit does not automatically adjust itself to a measured temperature. Feedback needs a measurement used to change the system, as when a thermostat controls a heater. A manual switch alone does not provide that automatic feedback.

quickCheck.prompt: Does an ordinary manual switch alone provide automatic temperature feedback?
options: No, measurement and a control response are needed
quickCheck.explanation: No, measurement and a control response are needed. A simple cell-and-lamp circuit does not automatically adjust itself to a measured temperature. Feedback needs a measurement used to change the system, as when a thermostat controls a heater. A manual switch alone does not provide that automatic feedback.

additions.title: Failure points
additions.objective: Identify a broken path as a circuit failure

content.body: A loose connection, broken wire or open switch can interrupt a series path. A lamp going out is therefore not enough evidence that its charge has been used up. Check the path and components to distinguish the possible faults.

quickCheck.prompt: A loose wire makes a series lamp go out. What is a likely cause?
options: The lamp has consumed all the charge
quickCheck.explanation: The conducting path is incomplete. A loose connection, broken wire or open switch can interrupt a series path. A lamp going out is therefore not enough evidence that its charge has been used up. Check the path and components to distinguish the possible faults.

additions.title: Trace the system
additions.objective: Trace current through a complete series path

content.body: The schematic uses one cell, one switch and two lamps in a single loop. With the switch closed there is a complete path. Opening that switch breaks the only path and stops steady current through both lamps.

quickCheck.prompt: Opening the switch in this series loop does what?
options: Leaves an independent path through each lamp
Breaks the only conducting path through both lamps
quickCheck.explanation: Breaks the only conducting path through both lamps. The schematic uses one cell, one switch and two lamps in a single loop. With the switch closed there is a complete path. Opening that switch breaks the only path and stops steady current through both lamps.
